captive_summary: Beacon Port was a proposed offshore deepwater-port LNG import terminal (concrete gravity-based storage tanks) roughly 45-56 miles off the Louisiana/Texas coast (Gulf of Mexico lease blocks High Island Area 27 / West Cameron 167). A Coast Guard/MARAD draft EIS described the platform-level concept design, but ConocoPhillips told USCG/MARAD in November 2006 it no longer had a business need and withdrew before a Final EIS/Record of Decision. No source found specifies how the isolated platform would have generated its own electric power.
confirmed_how: Oil & Gas Journal (2005) describes the proposed design: two concrete gravity-based LNG storage tanks, regasification equipment, docking platforms, a separate crew/equipment platform, and ~46 miles of new gas transmission pipeline, sized for 1.5 Bcf/d. MARAD's list of withdrawn/cancelled deepwater-port applications (Wayback-verified) confirms Beacon Port was withdrawn before a Record of Decision. Neither source, nor any other found, documents the platform's own power-generation arrangement (fuel type, turbine/genset spec, or grid tie of any kind, which is moot 45+ miles offshore).

captive_summary: Bradwood Landing was a fully FERC-reviewed onshore LNG import terminal on the Columbia River, Clatsop County, Oregon (single marine berth, two 9%-nickel-steel/reinforced-concrete storage tanks, 1.3 Bcf/d sendout, 36.3-mile pipeline to Kelso, WA). FERC issued a Final EIS (Aug 2007) and approved the project (Sept 2008) after a 3.5-year review with 109 mitigation conditions. The project was suspended for financing/permitting-delay reasons in May 2010 (developer NorthernStar Natural Gas filed for bankruptcy the next day), not for lack of a completed design. No source found documents the terminal's own electric-power supply arrangement (grid interconnection vs on-site generation, fuel type).
confirmed_how: Oil & Gas Journal: FERC approved the Pacific Northwest's first LNG terminal after a 3.5-year review, with 109 required mitigation measures. Offshore-technology.com (Wayback-verified) and The World Link (Astoria-area paper) corroborate the design (marine berth, two tanks, sendout pipeline) and the May 2010 suspension / bankruptcy filing. FERC's own FEIS docket landing page (bot-blocked live, Wayback-verified) is where the underlying engineering description -- including any power-supply section -- would live, but I could not access or search its full text within this pass's tool budget.

captive_summary: Broadwater was a proposed newbuild FSRU (1,215 ft x 200 ft, ~350,000 m3 storage) moored via a yoke mooring system roughly 9 miles off Long Island in New York State waters of Long Island Sound, with a FERC Final EIS (Jan 2008) and a Coast Guard Waterways Suitability Report. The U.S. Commerce Department rejected the project in April 2009 on Coastal Zone Management Act / scenic-value grounds before construction or vessel selection. No source found specifies the FSRU's onboard power-generation equipment or fuel (diesel vs gas/dual-fuel).
confirmed_how: FERC's Federal Register notice of the Final EIS (govinfo.gov, verified) describes the design in detail -- 350,000 m3 storage, berthing for carriers up to 250,000 m3, the yoke mooring system, ~21.7 miles of 30-inch pipeline, onshore facilities at Greenport/Port Jefferson -- but contains no power-plant description. Professional Mariner's rejection coverage gives vessel dimensions (1,215 ft x 200 ft, 80 ft freeboard, 90 ft operating depth) and notes seawater intake used partly 'for ballast, power generation and other uses,' but names no prime mover or fuel type. No turbine-vendor release or technical paper was found, consistent with the vessel never being selected/built before the 2009 rejection.

captive_summary: CE FLNG was a proposed small self-propelled FLNG export vessel to be moored on the river near Baptiste Collette Bayou, Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana. As of the last public status update found (September 2014), the project remained in FERC pre-filing (Docket PF13-11), awaiting a US Customs and Border Protection Jones Act ruling and restructuring to align with DOE export-authorization processes, with a formal FERC application still not filed (targeted for May 2015). No subsequent design/FEED-level publication was found -- treated as a cancelled proposal that never reached a published engineering design.
confirmed_how: LNG Industry's September 2014 update on FERC docket PF13-11 is the most detailed public status found: still in pre-filing, a formal application was targeted for May 2015, and startup was projected for Q1 2019 -- none of which materialized in any later reporting found. No equipment or power-generation specification was ever published for the vessel.

captive_summary: Calais LNG was a proposed onshore LNG import terminal (three storage tanks, ~1 Bcf/d sendout) and 20-mile pipeline on the St. Croix River in Calais, Washington County, Maine. It never advanced past FERC's Notice of Intent to prepare an EIS (Nov 2008 / supplemental June 2009) -- no draft or final EIS was ever completed. Financing partner GS Power Holdings withdrew in 2010 and FERC dismissed the application without prejudice in 2012. No engineering-level design, let alone a power-supply spec, was ever published.
confirmed_how: Bangor Daily News (2016): FERC's Calais LNG application 'was dismissed without prejudice by FERC in 2012,' grouped with Downeast LNG as having made 'essentially no progress' toward completing an application over a multi-year span -- i.e. the project never reached the EIS stage where an engineering design would be documented. Natural Gas Intel and the Federal Register NOI filings (Nov 2008, June 2009) confirm the project stalled at the pre-EIS scoping stage.

gogpt_candidate_basis: Never built; no engineering design was ever published for this site.

captive_summary: Calhoun LNG was a FERC-certificated (Final EIS Aug 2007, approval Sept 2007) onshore LNG import terminal at Port Lavaca/Point Comfort, Texas, on the Matagorda Ship Channel -- two full-containment storage tanks (5.7 MMcf each), ~1 Bcf/d regasification, and a 27-mile, 36-inch Point Comfort pipeline. The developer (Gulf Coast LNG Partners / KOGAS Canada / LG International / Port Lavaca LNG Services) filed with FERC in 2012 to abandon the project. No source found documents the terminal's own electric-power arrangement (grid tie vs on-site generation, fuel type).
confirmed_how: Oil & Gas Journal: FERC gave final approval for the Calhoun LNG project in September 2007, requiring commencement of service within 5 years. Offshore-technology.com (Wayback-verified) corroborates the storage/pipeline design (two 5.7 MMcf tanks, 1 Bcf/d capacity, 120 vessel calls/yr). Neither source, nor FERC's own FEIS docket landing page (bot-blocked live, Wayback-verified), addresses power supply in the sections I could access; the 2012 abandonment filing is confirmed but its text was not accessible to check for a power-supply mention.
